strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated problem: adapting RL fine-tuning to diffusion LLMs, where per-token likelihood estimation required by GRPO-style methods is intractable.

The formulation is principled: rather than reward maximization, DMPO targets matching the reward-tilted distribution via forward KL, implemented through importance sampling and a weighted denoising cross-entropy (WDCE) loss adapted from MDNS. The derivation connecting order-specific distributions (Eq. 8) to the WDCE objective (Eq. 11) is clean and correct.

The forward-only, off-policy design is a genuinely good fit for dLLMs: it avoids the expensive backward rollout-likelihood computation, enables replay buffers, and composes with fast inference techniques. This is a meaningful architectural insight distinguishing it from GRPO adaptations like diffu-GRPO and d1.

The analysis of the small-batch failure mode of forward KL (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 3) is insightful, and the weight baseline subtraction techniques, along with the approximate variance-reduction interpretation in Sec. B.2, are useful practical contributions. The ablation in Fig. 5 clearly shows the no-baseline variant fails to improve.

Empirical results are strong and consistent: DMPO outperforms d1 and pretrained dLLM baselines across GSM8K, MATH500, Countdown, and Sudoku at multiple generation lengths (Table 1), with particularly large gains on planning tasks. Training follows the same datasets, rewards, and hyperparameters as d1 for fairness, and d1 is reproduced from official guidelines.

The paper is well written and organized, with related work covering dLLM RL methods (diffu-GRPO, coupled-GRPO, UniGRPO, TraceRL, wd1, DiffusionNFT, FlowRL) and an appendix extending WDCE to zero temperature via proximal descent (Sec. B.1). Limitations are discussed honestly (single pretrained model, four benchmarks).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core WDCE machinery (importance-weighted cross-entropy for distribution matching) is adapted directly from MDNS (Zhu et al., 2025g) rather than introduced here; the main original contributions are the application to dLLM RL and the baseline-subtraction techniques. The paper is transparent about this, but the delta over MDNS and concurrent work (FlowRL, DiffusionNFT, TraceRL) should be articulated more sharply.

Evaluation is narrow: only one base model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct) is fine-tuned, despite Dream-7B being included as an evaluation baseline. Benchmarks are relatively easy/small-scale (GSM8K, MATH500, 4x4 Sudoku, 3-number Countdown), so it remains unclear whether DMPO scales to harder reasoning tasks, larger models, or other dLLM families. No comparison against other recent dLLM RL baselines (wd1, TraceRL, UniGRPO) in experiments.

The central motivation (mass-covering/diversity retention versus mode-seeking reverse KL) is asserted but not empirically validated: no diversity metrics, entropy measurements, or demonstration that DMPO yields more diverse high-quality responses than GRPO-style baselines. The claimed benefit of distribution matching is therefore only indirectly supported via accuracy.

The comparison with d1 is somewhat confounded: d1 uses SFT on s1k before diffu-GRPO while DMPO skips SFT, and Figure 4 shows d1 attains higher reward early in training. A head-to-head comparison with the same (no-SFT or matched) initialization would make the claims cleaner; the paper attributes early gaps to the missing SFT phase but does not disentangle this.

Weight baseline subtraction technically biases the objective away from the theoretically justified forward KL (acknowledged in B.2 as only approximate, since the ELBO surrogate replaces log p_theta), and the softmax-based real weights plus baselines introduce heuristics; there is no theoretical convergence analysis for the practical algorithm actually used. Sensitivity to key hyperparameters (temperature alpha, number of masked tokens, buffer frequency F) is not ablated.

Evidence of statistical reliability is thin: results appear to be single runs with limited error reporting; evaluation sets are small (e.g., 256 Countdown/Sudoku problems), and the training curves in Fig. 4/5 do not clearly indicate the number of seeds. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a fairly intricate implementation despite the detailed hyperparameters.

Claims about training-efficiency advantages (off-policy buffering, forward-only speed) are argued qualitatively but not quantified; no wall-clock or sample-efficiency comparison against d1 is provided, so the efficiency narrative is unsubstantiated by measurement.

strengths: The core idea of shifting from reward maximization to matching the full reward-tilted distribution is well motivated and cleanly formulated, and the paper connects it coherently to stochastic optimal control and the MDNS framework.

The WDCE loss is genuinely attractive for dLLMs: it is forward-only, off-policy-compatible, and avoids the intractable per-token sequence likelihoods that plague GRPO adaptations (diffu-GRPO's mean-field approximation is correctly identified as imprecise).

The paper is thoughtful about its own failure modes: the small-batch-size analysis (Fig. 3) and the three weight-baseline variants are sensible, with the model weight baseline given a variance-reduction interpretation in App. B.2.
The extension of WDCE to zero temperature via proximal descent (App. B.1) is a nontrivial and useful addition beyond the base framework.

Experimental details (hyperparameters, rewards, evaluation protocol, generation lengths) are reported at a level that supports reproducibility, and the limitations section is honest about the single-model, four-benchmark scope.
Results on planning tasks (Countdown +42.9% over d1, Sudoku +11.8%) show the method is not merely incremental on every benchmark.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the central technique (weighted denoising cross-entropy via importance sampling against a reward-tilted target) is directly adapted from MDNS (Zhu et al., 2025g), and the distribution-matching-vs-reward-maximization framing is concurrently pursued by FlowRL, wd1, and DiffusionNFT. The paper's contribution amounts largely to porting an existing sampler-training objective to the dLLM fine-tuning setting plus heuristic baseline subtraction.

The headline claims oversell the empirical gains. On the two most standard benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500), improvements over d1 are marginal (~1 point) and sometimes within noise; the dramatic +42.9% on Countdown comes against a strikingly weak d1 baseline (26.56 vs. 75.78), which is not explained. Only one seed per result is reported, with no variance or significance testing in Table 1.

The method's central motivation (mass-covering/diversity of the reward-tilted distribution) is never evaluated. No diversity metrics, no comparison of response distributions, no evidence that forward-KL matching avoids reward hacking or mode collapse relative to GRPO-style baselines — the anti-mode-collapse story remains purely theoretical/asserted.

Key theoretical machinery is approximate in practice: sequence log-probabilities are replaced by negative ELBOs, the partition function Z(q) is estimated from a small number of rollouts via softmax normalization, and the baseline-subtraction is justified as exact only under conditions (exact log pθ, fresh buffer) that do not hold. The accumulation of these approximations is not quantified.

Comparison fairness is debatable: d1-LLaDA includes an SFT phase while DMPO does not, yet the paper presents DMPO's modest math gains as superiority without isolating whether the off-policy replay buffer, the forward-only loss, or simply more training steps drive the differences; training duration (4,000 steps) and compute are matched to hyperparameters but the compute accounting between methods is unclear.

The empirical scope is narrow: one pretrained model family (LLaDA-8B), four benchmarks, no larger-scale models, no instruction-following or general-capability evaluation to check for regression, and no comparison against other concurrent dLLM RL methods (wd1, TraceRL, UniGRPO) beyond discussion in the related-work section.

The WDDO variant is introduced as a contribution but shown only in a single ablation (Fig. 5) where it destabilizes and collapses; it reads as an unfinished component rather than a validated technique.

No mention of code release, and the strong performance gap on Countdown relative to all baselines (more than 3x LLaDA-1.5) deserves more scrutiny/verification given it is the source of the abstract's headline number.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question—how to design RL fine-tuning for diffusion LLMs—with a principled alternative to GRPO-style reward maximization: matching the reward-tilted distribution via forward KL (cross-entropy), which is mass-covering and claimed to preserve response diversity.

The WDCE objective is well-motivated: it is off-policy (supports replay buffers), avoids the notoriously expensive per-token sequence likelihood estimation for dLLMs, and exploits the cheap forward noising process unique to masked diffusion. This is a genuinely interesting algorithmic direction distinct from backward-only GRPO adaptations.

The theoretical treatment is above average for this area: the appendix derives a proximal-descent generalization to zero temperature (B.1), interprets the weight baselines as approximate variance reduction via the score-function identity (B.2), and proves the global optimum of the WDDO objective (B.3). The importance-weight formulation for estimating the partition function Z(q) is training-free and clearly derived.

The diagnosis of the small-batch failure mode of positive-weighted CE (Fig. 3) and the proposed weight baseline subtraction (group/individual/model variants) is a concrete, useful practical contribution, supported by an ablation (Fig. 5) showing training fails without it.

Empirically, DMPO shows strong gains, particularly on planning tasks (+42.9% Countdown, +11.8% Sudoku over d1 at length 256), consistent improvements across three generation lengths, and higher training reward than d1. Experimental details (rewards, hyperparameters, LoRA rank, sampler settings) are reported thoroughly in Appendix C.
The limitations section is honest: single pretrained dLLM, four benchmarks, unknown generalization to other models and domains.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the WDCE loss is directly adapted from MDNS (Zhu et al., 2025g), and the reward-tilted distribution-matching view is well established in SOC and concurrent work (FlowRL, DiffusionNFT, wd1). The main new elements are the policy-learning adaptation and the baseline subtraction heuristics.

The central claims about diversity and mode coverage (mass-covering forward KL, 'exploring diverse high-quality reasoning paths') are asserted but never empirically validated—no diversity metrics, no analysis of response distribution entropy, and the comparison to reverse-KL mode-seeking is only qualitative (Fig. 2).

Evaluation is limited in scope: a single 8B model (LLaDA-8B-Instruct), four benchmarks, and 256-problem evaluation sets for Countdown/Sudoku with no error bars, seeds, or statistical significance testing. Only the group baseline is used for the main table; which baseline is used per task appears to be selected post hoc.

The comparison to d1 is confounded: d1 includes an SFT phase (s1k) before diffu-GRPO while DMPO does not, and training durations differ (4,000 vs up to 13,000 iterations). While this works in DMPO's favor, it makes the headline improvements difficult to attribute cleanly to the algorithm, and the pipeline difference is only partially discussed.

Approximations that could bias the method are acknowledged but not quantified: the negative ELBO is used as a surrogate for the exact sequence log probability inside importance weights, baseline subtraction with group/individual variants only approximately preserves gradients (B.2 admits the variance-reduction argument holds only approximately), and WDDO is shown to be unstable at scale in the authors' own ablation.

No code release is stated, which, combined with several implementation-sensitive choices (4-bit quantization, semi-autoregressive block sampler, mask-token count of 4, post hoc baseline selection), limits reproducibility.
The generalization claim (e.g., to Dream or larger dLLMs, and to the α→0 forward-only regime presented in B.1) is left entirely untested; the most theoretically interesting variant is not evaluated.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written reframing of dLLM RL fine-tuning: shifting from reward maximization to matching the reward-tilted optimal distribution via forward KL, which naturally addresses mode collapse and leverages dLLMs' forward noising process.

The WDCE loss is derived carefully, with a solid theoretical backbone: the SOC/CTMC derivation in App. B.1 provides an elegant justification that ELBO-based sequence-level matching is equivalent to path-level matching, which answers the most obvious technical objection (intractable sequence likelihoods in dLLMs).

The analysis of the small-batch failure mode of positive-weight losses (Fig. 3) is insightful, and the proposed weight baseline subtraction techniques (group/individual/model baselines) are simple, well-motivated, and empirically validated (Fig. 4).
Strong empirical results: DMPO substantially outperforms d1 and cGRPO across GSM8K, MATH500, Countdown, and Sudoku, with particularly large gains on planning tasks (+46.48% Countdown over d1).

Comprehensive efficiency analysis: off-policy buffer reuse (2–3x sample efficiency), up to 8x faster rollouts with Fast-dLLM, achieving d1-level reward with only 31% of the training compute, plus ablations over N, F, weight-baseline variants, and entropy/diversity analysis (Fig. 9).
Honest limitations section acknowledging that evaluation is restricted to one pretrained dLLM family and four benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited scope of empirical validation: a single dLLM family (LLaDA-8B), four relatively small benchmarks, and fixed generation length during training. Generalization to other dLLMs (e.g., Dream) and other task domains (coding, instruction following) is untested, weakening the claim of being a general dLLM RL method.

Headline improvements are somewhat inflated by cherry-picking: 'up to 54.3% over SOTA' comes almost entirely from Countdown, while gains on GSM8K/MATH500 are modest (+2–4%); the abstract's framing overstates the typical improvement.

The importance weight w(o|q;σ) still requires log pref/pv sequence probabilities, which are themselves ELBO-approximated; while App. B.1 argues path-level equivalence, the practical bias/variance of using a small number (4) of masked-token samples per sequence for weight estimation is not analyzed or ablated.
WDDO, one of the two proposed techniques for negative gradient insertion, shows instability after 1k steps (Fig. 4) and is not used in the main results, leaving its practical value unclear.

Fairness caveats in comparisons: d1 includes an SFT phase while the headline DMPO result does not (favorable to the authors), but conversely baseline numbers are all self-reproduced rather than reported, and no statement about releasing code/weights is provided, hurting reproducibility.

The zero-temperature variant (App. B.2) that would make the method fully forward-only sacrifices the diversity guarantee central to the paper's motivation and is deferred to future work, so the most practical configuration remains unexplored.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated: shifting dLLM RL from reward maximization (reverse KL, GRPO-style) to forward-KL distribution matching against a reward-tilted target, which exploits the forward noising process unique to masked diffusion models.

The derivation is carefully grounded: the SOC/CTMC formulation (Sec. B.1) connects the ELBO-based WDCE loss to path-level KL matching, and the paper is transparent that the ELBO surrogate makes the variance-reduction argument only 'approximate' (Sec. B.3).

The analysis of the small-batch failure mode of positive-weight cross-entropy objectives (Fig. 3) is insightful, and the three weight-baseline variants are sensible; the ablation in Fig. 4 clearly shows baselines are needed for training to progress.

The empirical study is relatively thorough for an RL paper: four tasks, three generation lengths, ablations over rollout count N and buffer frequency F, compute-matched comparisons (Fig. 5, PF-days), entropy/diversity analysis (Fig. 9), and evidence of stability with up to 24x stale data.
The off-policy/forward-only design is a genuine practical advantage for dLLMs, with a demonstrated ~3x sample-efficiency and ~31% of the training budget needed to match d1.
weaknesses: The central objective (weighted denoising cross-entropy via importance sampling against a reward-tilted target) is directly adapted from MDNS (Zhu et al., 2025e); the paper's contribution is applying it to dLLM RL plus engineering fixes, which is incremental. Concurrent FlowRL also targets distribution matching for LLM reasoning, weakening the framing novelty.

The advertised 'theoretical guarantees' are weaker than claimed in practice: the loss (11) replaces the intractable sequence log-probability with the negative ELBO, making the objective a biased surrogate, and the partition function Z(q) is estimated by batch softmax, which the authors themselves identify as the small-batch failure mode requiring corrective heuristics (weight baselines). The final algorithm deviates from the theoretically grounded objective.

Headline gains are somewhat overstated: the 'up to 54.3% over SOTA' comes from a single Countdown cell, while gains on the standard math benchmarks (GSM8K +2.40%, MATH500 +3.00% over LLaDA-Instruct) are modest, and comparisons across the three DMPO variants show large inconsistencies (e.g., Countdown 128: 67.19 vs 59.77 vs 54.69), suggesting variance that is never quantified (no multi-seed error bars for Table 1).

Missing empirical comparison to the closest recent dLLM RL baselines (wd1, TraceRL, UniGRPO) that are cited as concurrent/relevant; only d1 and cGRPO are evaluated. Some quantitative claims about stability of stale data rely on training-reward curves rather than held-out evaluation.

Generality is limited to a single pretrained model family (LLaDA-8B); Dream is only used as a frozen baseline. The authors honestly acknowledge this, but it materially limits the evidence that DMPO is a general method rather than tuned to one model.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters and datasets are documented, but no code release is stated, and evaluation details such as the number of evaluation runs and answer-extraction procedures for the accuracy numbers are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper offers a principled RL framework for dLLMs grounded in forward-KL / stochastic-optimal-control arguments, cleanly adapting the MDNS weighted denoising cross-entropy idea to policy fine-tuning; the SOC derivation in App. B.1 (path-level RN derivatives for CTMCs) is a genuinely useful theoretical justification for the ELBO approximation that is often hand-waved in this literature.

The identification of the small-batch failure mode of positive-weight objectives (Fig. 3) and the proposed weight baseline subtraction (Sec. 3.3) is a thoughtful, well-motivated practical contribution, with three sensible baseline variants and a variance-reduction interpretation in App. B.3.

The off-policy, forward-only nature of WDCE is a real algorithmic advantage unique to diffusion LLMs (replay buffers, no trajectory tracking), and the empirical efficiency results are convincing: 2–3× sample efficiency over diffu-GRPO, same reward as d1 with ~31% of the training compute, robustness to stale data (F up to 24), and 8× faster rollout sampling with Fast-dLLM (Figs. 5, 8).

The experimental section is relatively thorough for this setting: three generation lengths, two additional post-trained base models (LLaDA-SFT, LLaDA-1.5), ablations over N and F, weight-baseline comparisons, entropy analysis supporting the diversity claim, and reward dynamics vs. d1 (Fig. 6).
The limitations are honestly stated (single pretrained dLLM, four benchmarks), and related work, including concurrent efforts (FlowRL, DiffusionNFT, TraceRL), is covered fairly and precisely.
weaknesses: Generality is limited: DMPO is applied only to the LLaDA family; Dream-7B appears only as a fixed pretrained baseline, never fine-tuned with DMPO. Claims that DMPO is the way to do RL for dLLMs rest on a single model lineage, and the conclusion itself concedes this.

The headline gains are uneven. Countdown (+46% over d1) and Sudoku dominate the story, while GSM8K (+2.40%) and MATH500 (+3.00%) improvements over d1 are modest, within what could plausibly arise from training-budget differences (4,000 vs. up to 13,000 iterations for d1 reproduction). The abstract's 'up to 54.3%' framing cherry-picks the most favorable task.

There is a theory–practice gap at the core of the method: the baseline-subtracted loss (12) breaks exact unbiasedness of the importance-weighted forward-KL objective. The variance-reduction argument in B.3 only justifies subtracting the p̄θ/pv term (model baseline), yet the main results use the group baseline (13), which subtracts the constant 1 and is biased unless p̄θ/pv ≈ 1. This should be stated more directly.

Evaluation rigor has gaps: no confidence intervals or multiple seeds on Table 1; the Sudoku and Countdown test sets are only 256 instances, where the large reported gaps could be sensitive to sampling; and there is no significance analysis despite several results differing by 1–2 points.

Reproducibility is not adequately supported: no code release is mentioned, and while hyperparameters are given (App. C.2), several details critical to replication (e.g., exact buffer/weight computation under LoRA, fast-dLLM integration) are spread out or unspecified.

The central empirical claims (DMPO vs. d1) rely on the authors' own reproduction of d1 rather than published numbers under identical conditions; differences in LoRA rank, training length, and sampler settings between the two pipelines are possible confounds that are discussed but not isolated.
The WDDO variant (Sec. 3.4) is introduced at some length but is shown to be unstable (Fig. 4) and is not used in any main result, so its contribution to the paper is marginal.
